title: Alex Spatic on alto sax: Loyacano, Rudy Vallee, Toscanini
summary: Sal tells how he found a Alabama alto player, helped him get jobs, and his later career with Rudy Vallee.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Anybody that came to New Orleans, there was any way of musicians, they came around, Lloyd Cannon, to see Joe. Joe was great. So, Mr. Cuadagnino brought Al down the door around there. So, I heard Al playing man, the riff is saxophone in the room. They had a piano room there. I almost played the piano. I knew it wasn't Joe. He was at the train theater. I said, who was that guy? So, I went to the window and I see Al, and I was at home playing the piano, a company, and I was playing stand-up playing saxophone. I was out of the door. So, then I went inside. He started playing stuff like Louis-Weelde-Weelde stuff, see? Like Saxophobia or anything. They're great stuff, see? So, right away I said, well, we've got to get the guys out right now. The boy's great. He's from Alabama, you know. I brought him down to, what I'm telling you is why, if I was saying it wrong, she would have said, what the things going on then. So, when I had Joe like, and I believe, took him down to the world line, see? To sell a proper Reese or Howard, you know? I bought my first set of drugs from Howard's Boat Reese on time, man. I got him, see? So, we brought, we got a daughter out there, of O'Reese. So, O'Reese gave me a job right away, at the Belgrade Cards. He was good, man. Alex could practice, and I couldn't play with us, but he could play jazz. Too good for jazz, man. All that fair stuff, you know? Well, he played there a while. Then he went to the Orphan Theatre. In the Orphan Theatre, he went on strike. We went up north and he played with O'Reese Jones. Then he went with Rudy Valli, you know? And one time I was up in Oakland, I thought of him for the D&D D&D. One time I was up in the Al's, and Al was walking around the bar. I said, what you say, Al? He said, what you say, Al? I said, who you play with now, Al? He said, well, I used to live in Valet. He said, when I was there, I'd love a Toscanini. Oh, man. I said, you see where I went up there. Little of the station. Played fine shots.
No, no, he's in the studios now. He came down and taught at Loyola once. He did?
No, I haven't seen Al in years. His brother Pete plays good too. Not as good as Al, but he plays good. You know Pete, then?
I never met him, but I know who you're talking about.

He had a bat to fall in love for a while. He was going to play like Al, of course. There's not many guys like Al. What did Al play then? Alto. Alto. Did he play any clarinet or anything? Oh, yeah. I played any clarinet when I heard him.
Played in, huh? But he's still mainly alto. This is fine. I could play right in the place. You just got all this, man. You know, the old time guy.
